It may be that one statement is insufficient but a cumulative amount of such materials, he would be entitled to rely upon the truth of the background. As far as his criminal liability is concerned. What one's got to remember is that this issue concerns criminal responsibility and his criminal liability for matters that he either knew or should have known, would have had cause to have known, and those materials that this witness is producing go very much to a dimension of that issue. And that's all I have to address you upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I think that what Mr. Nice has asked, to keep back the documents which are the result of regular official, current, and at the time of the work -- at the time the work of one crime inspector who is testifying here, is completely unfounded. In fact, Mr. Nice has the right to ask all those questions to raise them during the cross-examination. That is the very purpose of cross-examination. It is in cross-examination that he is able to question the credibility of the witness and to try and raise that question. And in the cross-examination he can also bring up material facts, the ones that the witness is testifying to, and try to challenge those. Now, to try to eliminate and reject somebody's testimony and documents about the time that the witness is testifying about is completely unfounded, and I'm sure you're fully conscious of the fact that a large number of these documents came into being before the Racak case. Racak is a village in the territory of the Secretariat of the Interior in which at the time the crime inspector by the name of Jasovic worked. There weren't thousands of inspectors working there, just a few of them, and he was one of them. He and a colleague of his, they took the statements, and they compiled the documents, and those documents are presented here as evidence. Not documents which were compiled precisely for this procedure here but they were contemporaneous with the events that took place and the cases there. So they are official documents, they are documents which were the result of policework, and they are being tendered here through -- presented here through witnesses such as General Stevanovic who was the assistant minister of the interior, that is to say a high ranking police official, who is testifying about those events, both on the basis of documents that he had at his disposal and on the basis of the knowledge he had in view of the position he held and also in view of the fact that at that time on many occasions he was in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija himself. So there are absolutely no grounds for that. Secondly, Mr. Nice has been saying here that he has some knowledge or awareness or that he has some -- he knows that some witnesses took statements under coercion, under duress. I can guarantee that you're going to find as many witnesses as you like in Kosovo to testify to whatever you want them to testify to, but that is all geared towards the purposes here, not towards establishing the facts from the period of time that we're discussing here. And my second point is this: I'd like to draw your attention to a quite obvious matter, quite evident: A whole series of these statements which was taken by the Secretariat of the Interior of Urosevac and Mr. Jasovic and not confessions at all. They are information about others; other people, other circumstances, descriptions of whom they saw, who was armed, who were members of the KLA, who were not members, what colour the cars were, what they had equipment-wise, uniform-wise, where Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the bakery was, where the infirmary was. What kind of confessions are we talking about? They aren't. And I think that on the previous working day I presented a statement from one of the witnesses, a statement compiled by Jusuf Shefqet Becir was his name, Jasovic took it, and it showed that the two persons mentioned in that particular statement were members of the KLA from Kotlina. Today, on the other hand, we saw that in a document by Mr. Nice we have 12 names listed of KLA members from Kotlina. And in the document which was the result of Jasovic's operative work, two people were identified. In the document I received from Mr. Nice, 12 people are mentioned. Neither documents are complete because all the people over there were members of the KLA and they were clashing with the police forces there at that time, just like this book, the book that I offered up about the KLA with their names. I'm sure that's not complete and comprehensive either. It contains some names but not others. But at all events and at any rate, everything that was the result of official work as official documents along the line of duty in the police force which are being tendered as evidence here I believe should be admitted into evidence as such, and I think that it is quite untenable to disqualify a witness by saying that somebody subsequently tried to compile evidence that he exerted force and that witnesses were made to make statements under duress. And in none of those confessions -- they're not confessions, they're statements collected by Mr. Nice during the testimony Mr. Jasovic himself, one of the people giving the statements said they gave it when they saw bloodstained walls in the basement of the Secretariat of the Urosevac Secretariat. And Mr. Jasovic said that the secretariat in Urosevac did not have a basement or cellar at all, so I don't think there's any sense in following those lines and presenting arguments of that kind. Everything that Mr. Nice has to challenge he will be able to do so during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple of points, and -- there's always a danger in imputing to one's opponent a strategy or inviting an explanation for the process that leads to an action being taken, because it's always possible that the opponent will feel obliged to reveal and in view of what Mr. Kay said, I do. I made it clear that it was your recent rulings that stimulated my reflection on the problems we were facing. And I have very much in mind from the combination of recent rulings two points; one that seeking certification is not a proper way of expressing disagreement with a ruling, and I accept that; and second, that case-by-case decisions are what you're making. That led me to examine the difficult position in which we found ourselves and to come to the conclusion that I had erred by being too -- "accommodating" is the wrong word, but I hadn't been sufficiently adversarial, again something that I was invited, as it were, to reconsider by the rulings. And the problem we faced was this: If hearsay evidence that is challenged comes in on an important point, and obviously whether the victims at Racak were active KLA members is an important point, if it comes in in hearsay, I must be allowed under your Rules, under our Rules, Rule 95, to explore the issue of whether it should be admitted if it's been obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission is antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. Now, here's the problem, and if I may say so the only point, since I'm invited to reveal my strategy, the only point upon which we maintain a position contrary to any of Your Honours' recent rulings at all. Your Honours have said that we can't put in as an exhibit, to neutralise statement 1 of person X, we can't put in statement 2. It can't become evidence in the case. So that we are not in the position to cross-examine and to put exhibits in, because of course the witness will say "untrue" or "I know nothing about it." Probably does know nothing about the second statement. He can't know anything about it. And so that problem basically means, that combination of decisions, means that I can't challenge evidentially the grounds of admissibility, and that must be, in our submission, completely wrong. That's what made me go back to think about what would happen in an ordinary trial, and of course the answer is you would have a voir dire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you only have a voir dire, do you not, to get around the problem of perhaps the right to silence where, for example, the accused would have to give evidence to deal with a matter, which doesn't arise here. What -- how would you deal with this in a domestic court, this situation? You wouldn't, in the middle of a Defence case, seek a voir dire, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course in a domestic court you -- let me go back. I understand that the rules of hearsay have changed significantly and I haven't done a trial in our domestic jurisdiction with the revised rules of hearsay but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but you would have a witness -- forget hearsay, the witness says something and you've got a statement of what he said on another occasion. What you would do is you'd cross-examine him about it and then you would seek leave of the Court to lead evidence to prove the statement at an appropriate stage in the proceedings. You wouldn't be seeking an interruption of the Defence case to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour's, I think right. It's under Lord Denman's Act, isn't it, that there was an absolute right to cross-examine on a prior statement provided the circumstances of making the statement were revealed to the person concerned. But there we're dealing with something different. There we're dealing with Witness X in the witness box who says proposition A. I have a statement attributed to Witness X, signed or otherwise, written or otherwise, asserting the reverse. I am allowed to cross-examine him on it, and if he acknowledges that the signature is his, then it goes in. If not, then I have to call the maker of the statement to prove -- to prove that it was made. But that's not what we're dealing with. What we're dealing with here, and this is my problem as a litigator on this side of this courtroom, what we're dealing with here is a witness producing either firsthand - Jasovic - or secondhand - Marinkovic - or Nth-hand - Stevanovic - statements that plainly are being relied on for the truth of their content to prove these people were KLA. And indeed, as Mr. Kay was good enough to explain on a much earlier occasion, there is basically nothing I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You could try to lead the evidence in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then the -- I can, but should it -- should I be obliged to be in that position with the consequences that I have set out in various places when the evidence may be inadmissible because it's unreliable? If this Court has a rule that says unreliable evidence is inadmissible, then a party who holds evidence going to show that it is unreliable must be allowed to establish its unreliability. And that's all I'm seeking to do, and that's exactly the process, since Mr. Kay wants to know, that led to my making this application. Of course, this application was really to try and decide when we should have the argument, the full-blown argument. It's turned into the full-blown argument itself. As to His Honour Judge Bonomy's query in -- the position on voir dire trials has been dealt with in various cases and allowed as a possibility in the Appeals decision in Mucic, which you can find. Although there wasn't one, it was clearly expressed that that was a possibility. Yes, this was a case of a defendant's statement, an accused's statement, but I think the principles are general. There's a case from Rwanda called Bizimungu, an oral decision on the qualification of a Prosecution expert Rubaduka, and again that was found as a possibility, that you can have a voir dire. But the general proposition is, to which in my respectful submission the answer must be, yes, you can have such a hearing, the general proposition is if there is a provision that allows exclusion on the grounds of unreliability, then in certain circumstances it must be open to the opposing party to deal with unreliability by the calling of evidence. Now, here -- and then I must revert to the point about calling evidence in rebuttal and drawing your attention again to our assumption - maybe I was a party to the assumption, maybe it was my fault that I allowed the assumption to continue - the assumption that the rebuttal evidence would be the evidence of the witnesses themselves, or 20 or 30 or 90 of them. You know, it could be the evidence from the investigators, and I'm not going to rehash that argument. But my immediate problem is what to do about this particular witness. If -- I would prefer, obviously, that there should be -- if there is any question of my not being allowed a voir dire, then I would prefer the matter perhaps to be first the subject of a written argument - I've got one substantially prepared but not finally prepared - so that you can have a look at the authorities if you have any doubts on the matter and revert to it next week. And I don't need to deal with this part of the evidence with this witness this week, that's for sure, but it's certainly an important point and will have a significant affect on the scale of evidence that I may seek to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So at this stage your application is confined to seeking a ruling on Jasovic's evidence, testimony that relates to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Jasovic with this witness, which I would invite to be negative for this witness, knowing that it be dealt with with the other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not going to deal with any questions of admissibility now. Mr. Nice, you may put in your submissions on the voir dire by Monday, and we can have a response to that from Mr. Kay and the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Much obliged, Your Honour. Sorry to have taken a little more time than usual, but it's quite an important point, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness be called. There is one matter that should be dealt with. It's tab 177. Yes, tab 177, which has the names of rape victims, and that should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you may commence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Remind us, please, of your personal history. In 1990, what job did you have?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When giving answers on the first day, I think I explained what I did in which period. In 1990, I think I was head of the department of the police, or commander of special units of the police, and for a certain period of time I was in Kosovo and Metohija as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You remained head of the special units for how many years?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean commander of special units of the police? Well, it must have been four or five or even up to six years. Tentatively from 1990 until 1996. Tentatively.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. What police rank did you hold when you were promoted in 1995 to general?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a rank. I had the -- I had the top police rank at the time, which was chief inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so it was either as chief inspector or possibly as general that you were in charge of the special units at the time of the DutchBat's withdrawal -- is this the DutchBat's withdrawal from Srebrenica, is it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And which bit of the geography were you involved in in their withdrawal? Where did you meet them and look after them?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Dutch Battalion? Is that what you mean? On that day, I came to Bratunac, and I found the leaders of the Dutch Battalion there at the hotel, together with General Mladic and a few other officers of the army of Republika Srpska. An hour later, approximately, we crossed the bridge at Ljubovija, and with a certain number of policemen I provided security for that battalion through Serbia all the way up to the Batrovci crossing, which is in Srem, on the border with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, as general and probably still in charge of the special units, you changed jobs in about 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1996, I think, I became deputy head of the police administration, and then head of the police administration. When I became lieutenant colonel general, that should have been 1997. Then I was appointed assistant for -- assistant minister for the interior. I was appointed. It was an appointment, not an election.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And it was as assistant minister that you dealt with Kosovo in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, I was in charge of particular lines of work, and I presented a document in connection with that, what I was formally in charge of. And it is correct that in 1998 and 1999, as I've already said, I carried out certain assignments upon instructions from my minister in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the police service that you have served -- and you gave up being an active policeman in 2000, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 2001, the beginning of 2001. I haven't ceased being an active policeman, though. I am still at this point in time an authorised official, that is to say a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, for example, you have ready access to the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can always go to the Ministry of the Interior. I am employed at the police academy, but in accordance with the law, I have the status of an authorised official.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The service, the police service that you served, is it one of which you're proud?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when we speak of the police service, the MUP, be under no illusion, I'm asking you about all of the MUP. You're proud of everything of the MUP, are you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am proud of all the units that I belonged to. When I say that I am proud of the police that I belonged to, I primarily mean the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, yes, I wondered whether you might say that, because -- but on the other hand, do you remember an answer that you gave to the accused - I'm just trying to find the detail - right towards the end of your evidence, where you were asked about your knowledge of the activity of the police outside Serbia, and you said you knew absolutely everything about what they were doing. I'll try to find -- do you remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although you may for a period of time have been more intimately concerned with the public police, you know about what the DB did, don't you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know relatively little of what the state security sector did because these are two sectors that had a completely different scope of work and activity. Police conduct culture was that what the DB did was not supposed to be matter of in-depth interest for any one of us belonging to public security. In principle, generally speaking, I know what they did but I was never interested in great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was nothing they did of which you were ashamed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not do anything that I know of that they should be ashamed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That they should be ashamed or of which you should be ashamed? Mr. Nice -- I think the question was, "There was nothing they did of which you were ashamed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my understanding of the question. My answer is in respect of such a question. Actually, I have no reason to feel ashamed because I did not belong to that sector, and I do not know of anything that I should be ashamed of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We haven't got it translated, but would you take your tab 6, please. I should say the accused doesn't have it translated, because it's not our duty to do so. Now, I think I'm going to be referred to the correct clause, but you can take us there. There was, in fact, a duty for the two parts of the police service to cooperate, one with another, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's Article 17 and 20, I think. We won't take time with reviewing them now, but they require one part of the police service to cooperate with the other, and that makes it impossible for a very senior policeman like yourself to claim that you don't know what the other side is doing.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement is not correct. "Cooperation" means to give assistance in accordance with a concrete request and to notify the other sector if the other sector knows something from the scope of work of the former. Cooperation in the sense that you put it does not mean that one sector will know everything about the other sector. After all, state security -- the state security sector in a certain way, according to the nature of their work, is more closed than the sector of public security. It is logical that they know more about the public security sector than the public security sector knows of their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as paramilitaries are concerned, I have a number of questions to ask you, but at this stage just one. From your answers about paramilitaries, would it be really a matter of complete disrepute for a police officer like yourself ever to have worked alongside or with any paramilitary group?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my understanding and in the understanding of the top echelons of the ministry, that would be a bad thing or, rather, it would be unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, another little matter of detail. You told us about Mr. Paponjak, the traffic policeman who we heard from before you, and he produced us a tab, 2.4, an exhibit, and it was his exhibits tab 2.4, and you hadn't seen it yourself until it was shown you by the accused. Do you remember that? Any time you want to be reminded of something or have your memory refreshed, just tell me and we'll give it to you. We can hand you the document again, or you can remember it. And you told us that you had a conversation in the hotel with Mr. Paponjak about the exhibits. Do you remember that? And tell us again what it was he told you.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, may I say that we did not discuss exhibits. We talked in general terms about the dossier KiM, Kosovo and Metohija. So he helped me understand those letters and numbers, and he just told me that the letters denote subdossiers and that Roman numerals were used to denote secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would Your Honours give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did he say about the preparation of material for the indictment? Because I think you told us something about that.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Preparation of material for the indictment? That was my understanding, but -- that was my understanding of what you said, but in that case I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't got the immediate quotation to hand so I'll come back to that when I have, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mean 2.4?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "The information is not correct" "Response to point 7, or count 7"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If my memory is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right, yes. And Paponjak discussed that with him in the hotel, but we'll find the quotation and move on and we'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When these documents were produced, or these 4 or 500 documents, whatever it is, who chose them? Who selected them?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the documents from the tabs we just used, or do you mean the dossier on Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The very documents we've been using here in court. Who selected them?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents, to the best of my knowledge, were obtained pursuant to a request from the assistant for Defence, and I suggested in a general terms what documents could be sought, and that was three or four months ago. So the advisor for Defence, in fact. And I said what I could testify about, and then the advisors for the Defence drew up a list of documents to be requested from the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Were there any documents that you yourself produced?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no documents which I prepared myself, but there were a few documents which I provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us which ones?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I can't remember exactly now. I think that there were several tables. For example, the table that I mentioned about the terrorist attacks in the period from 1991 to 1997, for example, I had that one personally and I can remember that. But I will, of course, be able to tell you exactly what ones I had, although I can't remember just now. Some documents I did provide when I was interviewed in 2002, and so mostly it refers to that set of documents. But they were also obtained from the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the vast majority of the documents that are here beside you are documents produced by the ministry, and for the most part they were documents you'd never seen before?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. The first part of your observation is correct, and that is that the vast majority of the documents were produced by the Ministry of the Interior and just a small number, a negligible number, I provided myself, but those that I provided were copies of the ministry's to a certain extent and -- could you remind me of the second part of your question, please? The second part of your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you'd never seen before.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. Most of these documents I have seen before, and I've already explained that. I explained it when I was interviewed by your investigators already in 2002. If you look at the transcript, you will see that what I am saying is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we may have to look at that on a document-by-document basis, but let's deal with the documents of statistics that you've produced very generally. You're not a statistician yourself, are you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The statistical documents don't identify, I think, for the most part or any of them who created the document?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's a question.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps this was not explained in the previous testimony, but if I remember correctly, I think I did say that the statistics and tables were compiled by the analytics department of the Ministry of the Interior on the basis of official cases and case files that the ministry had and on the basis of reports from the staff in Pristina, and they received daily reports, as I've already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So I'm right; we can't actually get to the individual who bears responsibility for the compilation of the statistics, can we?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't know what person in particular compiled them, but I knew -- know who is at the head of the organisational unit in the ministry who was responsible for everything that that unit and department in the ministry did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've been provided with no original sources nor indication that we can have access to original sources?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't help you there. The advisors for Defence, I'm sure, would know who could help you. The only way I could help you is to tell you who you could contact for information about that, and I'm quite certain that the information will be as I've just stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't have, for example, criteria for how things were determined to be terrorist or non-terrorist, do we?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we don't have them specifically written down, but it is logical that experienced analysts and leaders in the secretariats deal with things of that nature and are able to qualify an act in the corresponding way. Of course, we can always raise the question of whether that way is the right way, but according to all our criteria, I think that the qualifications are good ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We know nothing of any electronic system for holding material or the way in which that system was accessed, do we?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, had I known and had I had the right or, rather, had I known what nature your questions would be, perhaps I could be of -- could have been of assistance to you and I could have brought in exhibits of that nature, but I didn't do so because I didn't know, so I cannot answer your questions. I quite simply don't have the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, how long did it take you to become familiar with this 17 volumes of documents as they are now? How long did it take you to become familiar with them and in order to prepare for giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat in part what I've already stated: The vast number of these documents that are here, that we have here, were known to me back to the days of the war. For example, Pusto Selo, Kotlina. I had information about that. And then again a number of documents I saw in the MUP before I moved to the police academy. And to be quite frank, I didn't have sufficient time to become well acquainted with all the exhibits and documents because I had to remind myself of some things and a lot of time has gone by since those things took place. But I can tell you now that I did not have a chance to look through all the documents in my preparation for testimony here, but from what I was able to look at and study, they are documents which are original documents of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you answer the question: How long did it take to prepare?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been here since the 13th of April. Perhaps you didn't know that. And if you want me to answer how long I would have needed, I would certainly have needed much more time. But the time that I had at my disposal I used in the best way I thought possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And just finally on this, as you were preparing -- and this is for a matter that doesn't relate to your evidence, understand. While you were preparing these documents, and I don't want to know anything about the detail of it, just help us: Were detailed notes being taken of the ways in which you could help with the giving of evidence as you were going through these documents?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not make any notes. Perhaps I did jot down a few things, and the notes that I made are in my room, but that is a limited number. Just enough for me to recall a date, a period, and so forth, because I have -- I find it quite difficult to memorise dates and numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The quotation that -- the quotation that I wanted to remind you of in relation to your knowledge of the DB as well as the public security was this: You were asked whether you were aware of each and every engagement of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia outside the borders of the republic; the time, the composition, all the details that have to do with these engagements, and you replied, if I may say so, emphatically, "I am aware of all the engagements of the police of Serbia outside the territory of the Republic of Serbia." That is your position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that includes not just public service deployment but also DB deployment, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer does not include the DB. Therefore, I said the police. And very often in public communication the police and MUP are used as synonyms, but I always like to refer to the police because the concept of the MUP, it is difficult to bring in to context and relationship with the operations that I was discussing during my testimony because the MUP implies the administration as well. It also includes the administration. And then this concept does not correspond to what we're talking about here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Now -- just to revert to and complete what I wanted to ask you about your conversation with Paponjak, you said this: You spoke of the dossier and the subdossier, including one based on allegations in the indictment. And you went on to say, "And I know that the ministry asked the secretariats to provide the ministry with all evidence and information concerning incidents described in the indictment that they might have anything about. That is what I'm absolutely certain of." His Honour Judge Bonomy asked you, "How do you know that?" And you said, "I know because while I was preparing to testify here, I spoke to certain people, including Mr. Paponjak, while we were at the hotel." So may I take it that your understanding from Paponjak was that the documents he was producing, or some of the documents he was producing were because the ministry had asked the secretariat to provide evidence and information concerning incidents concerned in this accused's indictment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that question is far too complex. It's too complicated and I'm not sure that I'm going to answer it properly, but I'll do my best. In continuation of my answer to a subsequent question, I said that I just mentioned Paponjak as a current illustration, but of course my preparation for testimony didn't begin when I arrived here, which is to say that certain elements about the Kosovo and Metohija dossier is something that I knew about before I talked to Paponjak, because these documents, this material is about that, and I -- it was I who brought these materials. And the second point is this: Before I talked to Paponjak, I knew, roughly speaking, orientation-wise, what the structure of the Kosovo and Metohija dossier was. I couldn't reconstruct it to any precision, but I did know that dossier A, for example, with cases resulting in death, I knew then that and know now, and that B are crimes are to the detriment of Albanians, with Albanians as victims; that the next one in line was against Serbs, where the Serbs were victims, but I couldn't remember the rest. So in responding to a question here, I recognised the letter DJ, and from the title of the piece of information I was able to conclude that it was a subdossier which related to events from the indictment. So that was the substance of my answer. And I have no changes to make to that answer. Quite possibly the answer wasn't clear enough, or was slightly complicated, but there you have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The original answer was very clear. The position now is extremely complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And perhaps you'd like to think back, Mr. Stevanovic. As His Honour Judge Bonomy observes, your answer was extremely clear. Let me just remind you of a little bit of the history of the questioning. The accused asked you in a question which was leading in form whether the document you were being shown related to an indictment other than his indictment but you maybe didn't hear the question and you made it clear that the document you were looking at related to this very indictment. When asked how you knew that, you made it quite clear you got that from a conversation with Paponjak. Do you now wish to change that simple explanation?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the way I put it, as you have just told us, then of course I could correct myself somewhat, but I didn't understand myself to have put it the way it was put. I don't doubt the interpretation, but I'm just wondering whether it was the right one. I know, also from Belgrade, that there is a subdossier which relates to the collection and amassing of facts by the secretariat from Kosovo which relate to the events from the indictment, and I explained at the time that the police used all sources available, and one of those sources was the indictment and knowledge of the indictment, and that source was that -- and therefore we wanted to amass the documents in one place, related to that. I'm very sorry. I thought I was clear enough, but it would appear that I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, what you say is interesting, but let's approach its value in this way: You and the accused's associates and advisors had no difficulty whatsoever in getting any documents you wanted from the Ministry of the Interior, did you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had any difficulties or not. I think they did. And I don't think they received all the documents they had requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But if your answers are correct, within the ministry there is a complete dossier, or there's -- it may not be complete, but there is a dossier specifically prepared with this litigation in mind, because it's prepared to deal with the allegations in this litigation. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely not correct about that. That dossier contains at least ten subdossiers and they are classified - and I've said this several times - according to set criteria which that working group applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a subdossier exists which is prepared with this litigation in mind because it deals with the allegations in this litigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It deals with the events from the indictment, and those events from the indictment are serious both in terms of how they are described and qualified and what it says there. It's quite natural that the MUP, which at the time of their occurrence was in charge, and is still in charge in one way for those events because they took place when the MUP had jurisdiction there to deal with those cases, but the MUP doesn't deal only with those events. It deals with all crimes, everything that is -- all acts against the war -- against the law. And it seems to me that it was a good idea. It seems to me a good thing that all these questions in the indictment are dealt with within one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two other points and I must move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to break at 20 minutes to, resume at 6.00, and then we'll have one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is well known, isn't it, that the allegations against the accused include that he committed serious crimes through the agency of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should like to ask you -- I'm not accustomed to this type of questioning, these questions, the way in which they're structured, I mean. Of course from the indictment we can see that the police had a significant part in the alleged events as described in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And my last question before the break, if this is convenient to the Court, is this: In your long evidence, you've heard on several occasions one or other of the learned Judges invite the accused to consider having called someone closer to the action than you, and on each occasion you will have heard the accused say he doesn't need to call anyone else. Do you understand, Mr. Stevanovic, that you are basically here to cover and deal with all allegations made against the accused on the basis of agency of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I of course did not think along those lines, and I have no awareness of that being the case. I decided to respond to the request for me to come here and testify and have declared that I will speak the truth. I of course answer questions, I don't formulate the questions. So I will be ready to answer all your questions just as I answered all the questions posed to me by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just clarify. When the witness said that he's not accustomed to this type of questioning, these questions, I gather that he was saying that some of the questions are posed as statements in the way in which we pose questions, certainly in common law jurisdictions, and so that's why he's saying he doesn't -- he's not accustomed to those type of questions, and that's certainly the way that you pose your questions. They're in the form of statements, and I'm very familiar with that way of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shall endeavour to highlight the interrogatory nature of my interrogatory statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Immediately before the break, I asked you whether you appreciated you were here to cover all aspects of the police case, and you said you weren't aware of that. In light of the questions you've asked, I'm going to seek your assistance on many topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Nice is asking improper questions to the witness because his question contains the assertion that the witness wanted to cover all aspects of the MUP, and that's not true. You know that before that there were other MUP representatives here. And secondly, your suggestion, to which Mr. Nice refers, that is to say that somebody who is closer to the events should be called, and I said that in that case that would not be necessary, that referred to a suggestion from you while we were showing photographs from Kotlina, which were taken on the day that the event took place, and I said that I assumed there was no need for somebody to come in, somebody who had taken the photographs and was in Kotlina. From that, we cannot deduce the conclusion that Mr. Nice has extracted at all and ask the witness to answer -- and said that he was the only person from MUP. There were Jasovic as crime inspector, then Paponjak was secretary. Now we have the assistant minister here. So he's asking quite the wrong questions and improper questions and leading the witness astray, trying to mislead the witness, in fact, and he is aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let us hear Mr. Nice's question. If it is improper, we'll exclude it. What's the question, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next question has changed and it's this:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you the officer who led the -- I was going to use the word "attack" -- that led the troops, the police troops in Racak? Were you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was not. And I answered that, that I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that man still alive? Goran Radosavljevic, is he still alive?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you either the officer or the prison service warden in charge of Dubrava prison at the time of the alleged bombings? Not the alleged bombings, the bombings. Were you? Of course you weren't. Are those men alive? Well, we know the assistant warden's dead. But others are alive, aren't they? Aren't they?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd once again like to ask you not to ask me questions the way you have been doing, because in the Serbian grammar, if I say "yes," then that would be a negation and would mean no. If I said "no," it would turn out that my answer was "yes." So could you ask me questions that I can understand straightforwardly? You have double negations, double negatives, and if I add my negative this is very convoluted then and complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I've made my point. I'm going to move on. You've taken the solemn declaration here.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've taken the solemn declaration. Are you prepared to help this Chamber if I give you that opportunity a little later? Are you prepared to help them? Or are you here to help the accused?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that. I am here to answer questions both put to me by the Defence and the Prosecution, and I will answer them by telling the truth. As to your previous question, I really can't give an answer because it seems to me to be nonsensical whether I was the warden of the Dubrava prison. I don't see the sense of that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In light of your answer that you're prepared to help this Chamber, would you be so good as to give us a list again of the paramilitary groups of one kind or another of which you were aware that operated in and from the territory of Serbia during these wars. Name them.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that it is important that we understand the concept as I understood it and put it. Only in that way am I able to answer your question. So the way I understand the concept, we're dealing with groups wearing military uniforms, with military weapons, which were not under the command of the regular military or possibly police forces. I cannot list all the groups. I can't enumerate them. I know some of their names, but I cannot say whether at that point in time they were within the composition of some structures, state structures or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... do your best.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the Serb Volunteer Guards, for example, and I said that I knew that it came within the composition of the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina, so at that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next name. Just the list. I just want the list, please, of the most famous paramilitaries. You gave us a list before and I want you to have another go.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, if I recall correctly, about the existence of the White Eagles, but I can't say who they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about certain paramilitary groups in the Republic of Croatia, such as the ZNG, for example, and in Krajina the Red Berets of Captain Dragan, for instance. I also know about Sarajevo and the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any other names come to mind?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can't remember any more just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the second time that you've given a list and on each occasion you haven't mentioned the Skorpions. Would you like to think about the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know about that particular paramilitary unit, but I don't know who it belonged to or whether it belonged to any regular state structure or not. And thank you for reminding me of it. If you remind me of some more, I'll be happy to answer you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It answered to the MUP, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, that it reported to MUP --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, tell the Court this --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- answered to MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- are you aware of the publication in your own country of reports to the effect that a video exists showing that Skorpions killed innocent victims at Srebrenica? Are you aware of that? It's been the subject of wide publicity.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that is something I absolutely do not know about, and I'm quite sure that a group with that kind of name was never active within the composition and structure of the police of the Republic of Serbia. Possibly certain individuals were taken on in some kind of procedure, but I claim that no organised group with a name of that kind ever belonged to the police of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what did the Skorpions do, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they did. I think they belonged to either police -- the police of the Republic of Srpska Krajina or the army of Srpska Krajina, and that's how I seem to recall that name and that particular group. I think it was in Slavonia, Eastern Slavonia or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. And if I give you an opportunity in due course to assist in identifying people on a video showing what may be the Skorpions killing in Srebrenica, will you assist me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In what way, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Identification of individuals, and other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you assist me? Now tell us -- you nodded. Now tell the Court this: Had you been aware of the publicity given to the possible existence of this video in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw a video of that kind. Therefore, I state --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of publicity given in newspaper articles to the possible existence of such a video? Indeed, it led to people being threatened and I don't know whatever else. Were you aware of such publicity? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be more specific: I absolutely don't know about any publicity linked to any kind of group bearing the name of Skorpion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sure that's --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, I can't know what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, you can help me with the next topic because I want you to describe your state or the country in which you lived for the decade of the 1990s rather more fully than we have done so far. Dealing with things politically, and you rose to the position of an assistant minister, throughout your time in the police in the 1990s, would it be fair to say that decisions as to what happened -- decisions of importance of what happened so far as the police were concerned and the army were concerned all ultimately channeled back to this accused, whatever the formal structures? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that statement. May I answer the first part of what you said now? I was not appointed assistant minister according to a political term. I put on a police uniform the first time when I was 14 years old. At the time when I was in the ministry, there were no political appointments as far as assistant ministers were concerned. Everybody appointed to that position would have a long service in the police force. Only ministers came from the ranks of politicians. And indeed throughout my professional career, I never dealt with politics. I dealt with law enforcement. I did not pass laws. I was not a member of parliament. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll ask the second part of the question: Did decision-making throughout the 1990s and whatever the structures, did decision-making of important decisions ultimately rest with this accused?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All decisions and all instructions that I received and carried out exclusively came from the minister of the interior while I was assistant minister. When I was at lower positions I received them from my immediate superior. I never got any instructions from President Milosevic in any way. I was never asked by him to come and see him, and I never went to see him, either at his invitation or because I wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You had access to a lot of material over the years. You know the general nature of the allegations made against this accused. Do you accept that serious crimes were committed by any Serbs in any of the theatres of war that we are concerned with here?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept as a possibility that there were crimes in all areas and that representatives of all sides took part in the commission of these crimes. However, a crime is a crime when it is proven and when a verdict is passed. I am a policeman. I don't like thinking in those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Assuming that such crimes were committed, from all your vantage points of knowledge, can you point us to any other senior politician or general, or whatever else it may be, who you could see as making independent judgements leading to the commission of crimes other than this accused? Can you point us to any individual who you say may have been responsible for the commission of the crimes that you accept may have happened? And, if so, who?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that kind of question because I do not have information. I have already said that I was not involved in any way in political decision-making. I said what meetings I attended, and I can testify to what I know from those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You and the accused had an exchange of some comparatively lighthearted nature about the use of the term "policeologist" which has been associated with Mr. Babovic. Although I can't find his using the term, it was used in a question by the accused of Zoran Lilic. It may well be that it did turn up in the evidence of Mr. Babovic and it hasn't been -- or isn't retrievable on our system at the moment. Have you read Mr. Babovic's report?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you like to tell us whether you -- or have you got a copy of it with you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps there is one somewhere, but I simply can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you make any notes on it to record where you assert or would wish to assert that he was in error?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not make any longer notes. Possibly on my own copy I jotted down a thing or two, perhaps a question mark or a statement of my own, but I cannot show that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you remember, so as we can deal with it, any part of his report that you say is fundamentally wrong?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I cannot recall in detail, but many statements and qualifications pertaining to the police of Serbia in the 1990s in my firm conviction are absolutely incorrect. They are political qualifications, rather, of an opponent of the then police rather than serious analytical conclusions of a serious analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you read his books?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In engaging --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not even know of the existence of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In engaging in the little dialogue with the accused where the word "policeologist" was bandied about, did you remember what job Mr. Babovic had before he retired?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you think --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Mr. -- you know, I've been in the police a long time but I don't know exactly what duty he had. I know that he worked at the Federal Secretariat for Foreign Affairs -- sorry; Internal Affairs. I always make this particular slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He became head of the Yugoslav Central Bureau of Interpol. Do you think such a person might have less or more knowledge of other police forces than you? Would working for Interpol give more or less access to other police forces than being a simple -- not simple, a straightforward, internal policeman?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you've assisted me, but I would like to know for how long he worked in that position. I know roughly what that sector in the Ministry of the Interior dealt with. If he was actually there, then I can claim with certainty that I have a better knowledge of the police of Serbia than he does, because that sector in the Federal Ministry of the Interior practically dealt in corresponding with Interpol in relation to particular events, but they never took part in investigating and resolving criminal cases. That sector in the federal MUP was a purely administrative organ within --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause. The question was whether he had more knowledge of other police forces. Would you accept that he did? Of other police forces; foreign police forces.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot answer that question because I do not have any information what the man personally dealt with. That sector does not deal with the structure and organisation of other police forces. They only cooperate with those police forces in respect of concrete events and concrete crimes in terms of legal aid, the exchange of information, et cetera. They do not analyse other police forces except if he himself did that by way of his own professional commitment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, his conclusions included that for the period between 1988 and 2000 the police had become an instrument for defending the regime from the people, that it was politicised, militarised, corrupt, and uncontrolled by society. Now, if you've read his report - we don't have time to go through it in detail, but if you have read it - would you like to think of any of the workings of the report that led to those conclusions that you can tell us to be wrong?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what you quoted just now speak in itself of a qualification that is not based on specific facts. Nothing is explained beforehand, and yet that kind of conclusion is reached. So there is no background given. I claim that the police was not politicised in Serbia, that it was not militarised in Serbia. I claim that it was not there to protect the state from the people. The police equally protected the people and the state, because that is what it's supposed to do according to the law and the constitution. Of course it is always possible to make certain contradictions, that the police protect people more than the state and vice versa. Policework is very delicate, and somebody can qualify it one way and somebody else can qualify it in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Do you --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police has to apprehend perpetrators of crimes and defend institutions. That is its duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember that in 1997 Nebojsa Sarkic was deputy Serbian justice minister?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I remember that. I remember for sure but I'm not sure of the exact period, but I'm sure it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... by Mr. Babovic, along with a lot of other material, but he is cited as having said in 1997 of the police force of which you are proud, this: "It is quite clear that the police are out of control. It is time for a large meeting like the fourth plenum, or something like that, to find ways of introducing control and punishment of the police." Now, can you explain what circumstances could lead your own deputy justice minister to give that summary of the police force of which you were proud in 1997?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to repeat yet again that I am proud of the police that I was in and where I was a person in charge. I read that before, and truth to tell, I don't believe even now that he actually said that. If he did actually say it, it is an absolute falsehood, and it is motivated by something that I am not aware of. I think even at this point in time that is not his view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question about Mr. Babovic is this: He retired, author of books on the police and Yugoslavia and other things, he retired in part because he had a clash with people from the Ministry of the Interior but also because he realised that things were happening in the country about which nobody knew and about which nothing was being done. As a policeman, retiring for those reasons. Can you understand his concerns in 1991?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I do not know that these reasons were actually correct. I don't know until when he worked and when he retired. And of course I cannot have any opinion as to his motives. If that is what he said his motives were, then it seems to me that he was not being sincere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that your state was not a police state. What definition of "police state" are you applying when you give us that evidence?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that concept can be understood in different ways, of course. In my interpretation of this concept, a police state would mean that the police played a dominant role, a very large police force, et cetera, frequency of repressive police measures and the like. I assert that in Serbia everything that was done in the 1990s cannot be qualified as a police state. We have had -- we had indeed a very complex security situation in the country, and it was very hard to do the right thing all the time. I'm a participant and witness of and in all of that. I know that we worked day and night in order to secure law and order and peace. And you know full well what kind of problems Serbia faced during those years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of the characteristics of a police state - would you accept this - is that it is anti-democratic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I accept that that would be a characteristic of a police state. Let me be specific. I do not accept that that was the case of the Republic of Serbia in the last decade of the 20th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another would be that the police have extensive if not almost unrestricted powers and are objects of fear to the population. Yes?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could accept that characteristic, too, but I assert that that was not the situation in the Republic of Serbia. The police in Serbia had the usual powers and authority prescribed in most European countries and for most European police forces according to what I've read and what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about the police in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police in Kosovo, regrettably, was in the most delicate position to defend part of the territory of Serbia from growing terrorism, which was not only a problem for the Republic of Serbia. It will become quite evident that that is a problem for the international community as well. The struggle against terrorism, as we all know from our experience, is not simple at all. I provided part of this explanation in my answers to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you accept --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you accept that Kosovo Albanians, by the end of the 1990s, if not earlier, much earlier, certainly by the end, would have been in fear of Serb policemen?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that there were Albanians who lived in fears of different kinds, but I'm convinced that they lived in greater fear of terrorists than of the police. I'm also convinced that for the most part fear from the police was imposed upon them by the terrorists, because that was part of the plan, that Albanians as citizens of Serbia should lose confidence in their state. That could not be the objective of the police by any means. The objective of the police was to keep this confidence, to raise it to a higher level, to build that confidence, and that is the conclusion that can be drawn from my testimony before this Court, and that can also be concluded from the documents that we presented to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going suggest to you now so you can know it's coming that in Kosovo in particular life became the life of a police state by the end of the 1990s and you know that to be true. Follow? That's the general suggestion.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, allow me to say that I know the situation in my country better than you do. I'm sorry if I'm overstepping my rights before this Court of law in saying that. I spent over five years in Kosovo and Metohija, and I know what effort and what sacrifice the police made in order to ensure law and order and confront terrorism. Of course, the saddest thing of all, in my personal opinion, is that some forces sided up with terrorism instead of siding up with the state in its struggle against terrorism. That is my greatest disappointment from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Returning to the proposition that a police state is anti-democratic, in democratic states exposure to criticism is a healthy thing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if it is sound and realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For a long time there have been non-governmental organisations that have had the courage to confront what's been happening in Serbia and Kosovo and to make their findings public, haven't there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were non-governmental organisations that were highly critical of the activity of the police in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Humanitarian Law Centre was one, the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights in Serbia was another.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know these organisations, but I have not dealt with them seriously although I did read some texts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we know from your answers yesterday that your duty as a police force would be to inquire into any allegation of crime, from wherever it came, to take it seriously and to look into it; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two points first of all: Where those two non-governmental organisations have drawn to the public's attention wrongdoings by Serbs - and they also bring to the public's attention wrongdoing by Albanians and anyone else - has your police force investigated their allegations or not?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which concrete allegations you have in mind, but I can give a general answer that all allegations regardless of their source get police attention and are investigated by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there's no reason, is there, to doubt the good faith of people who put themselves and indeed their lives at risk in exposing that which your society was unwilling to have uncovered? No reason to doubt their good faith, is there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again the question is a bit complicated. Perhaps I cannot follow it. I do not know people, at least from the police structure, who wanted something not to be uncovered. We did everything within our possibilities to discover everything that was illegal and to do on account of that everything that any police would have to do. Since we're talking about non-governmental organisations, first of all I have to say that I absolutely support the existence of non-governmental organisations, and I am aware of the role they play in any democratic society. However, over a certain period of time it is my impression we had highly partial conclusions drawn by some non-governmental organisations regarding the human rights situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not these two. You didn't know anything about them. You've told us that.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I knew nothing about them. I said that I knew of their existence and I said that I read some of the texts of those organisations. I'm worrying now about the interpretation, whether it's good since you're putting this kind of question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your diary, Exhibit 404 -- tab 404, just lay this one page on the overhead projector. 440, I beg your pardon. We can see on the left-hand side there, in a list of actions and other things, we can see -- and if there's an English translation, it's on page 39, but I don't want to take time duplicating because we can see it there. For the --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have a request, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... lines down, it says "Our enemies --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the last passage be redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back to the beginning of the 1990s. The SAJ, when was that formed? Tell us what it was and when was it formed.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are specialist -- it's a special anti-terrorist unit, the SAJ, which before that had a similar name but slightly different - I can't remember it now - and I know that it was established in 1978. That's when it was formed. And that it has existed to the present day and does exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: PJP was formed when, first formed when?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The PJP under that name -- well, I can't remember exactly. I think we had a document about that. So it could have been in 1993, for example, because the last document --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Early 1990s. The JSO, which became the Red Berets -- the JSO, which became the Red Berets, when was that formed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't finish my answer with respect to PJP and when that was formed. The first special purpose unit in Serbia was formed in 1972 and all subsequent ones nurture the traditions of those first units. And the JSO - I think I answered that question yesterday - it was formed in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Its precursor was formed in 1991.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Aren't you? We'll come to that very shortly. All of --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but just a moment, let me be specific because I don't want you to say that I'm sidestepping the issue. I just heard at an interview I had in Belgrade two or three months ago that Mr. Franko mentioned the formation of that unit in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that was a leading question. I said, "Well, if Franko said that, I have no reason to doubt it." That is quite right, that's what I said. But I know that the unit was formed in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These three units were all military in formation, weren't they? Military equipment, military structure.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not, of course, military units. However, internally and organisationally, as we call it, they had what we call military structure, but they weren't military units as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... early 1990s, right up and until 2000, or it may have been 2001, when the gendarmerie was formally introduced, you have an army, a police force which is functioning perfectly well, and at least three militarised or military characterised units. Now, can you explain why it was necessary to have these additional military-type units operating on the territory without formalising them as a gendarmerie, right through the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's quite clear. It's easy to explain that. Each of these three units was specific in one way or another and had its set purpose. So the special units were units which had more men. We said they were ad hoc units, not classical units of permanent composition, and they performed very different assignments, from the simplest task to provide security for public -- large public meetings, or more complex tasks, for example, to suppress and prevent terrorism. But let me repeat: They are not special units. Special anti-terrorists units -- unit was a small unit numbering 100 men, and that particular unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you now accept that Frenki, if he said he formed his unit in 1991, must have done so, and on your account done so without telling you about it or without your knowing about it? You described the Red Berets yesterday as paramilitary. Paramilitaries working on well-ordered societies have a destabilising effect, don't they? Can you explain to us, please, why it was necessary for a paramilitary force under the MUP to be operating from 1991?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you really have asked me five questions in one, and I'm not able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I'll ask you one question: Why was it necessary to have a paramilitary force acting under the MUP on your territory from 1991?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you a quite clear answer: Within the composition of the MUP of Serbia, there was never any paramilitary force active.
